claims.text: Rapid quenching after high-temperature synthesis preserves a homogeneously mixed, high-entropy state in noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles.
Rapid quenching preserves homogeneity by suppressing differences in the reduction rates of individual metal precursors.
Differential precursor-reduction rates would otherwise cause phase separation.
The proposed starting material is a uniformly mixed noble-metal precursor blend whose elements have differing reduction potentials.
High-temperature exposure induces decomposition of the metal precursors.
High-temperature exposure promotes atomic fusion and mixing of the constituent elements.
Rapid cooling freezes in an atomic-level homogeneous nanoparticle configuration.
At high temperature, all metal precursors form a liquid or near-liquid state in which their atoms are well mixed.
A rapid quench kinetically traps the mixed state as a single-phase nanoparticle.
Slower cooling gives the elements time to reduce at different rates and consequently form separated phases or elemental clusters.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will be single-phase, uniformly alloyed, and minimally segregated relative to slowly cooled nanoparticles.
Slowly cooled nanoparticles will exhibit phase separation or uneven elemental distributions.
The proposed mechanism should apply to noble metal–based HEA systems made at high temperatures when entropic stabilization and kinetic trapping are significant.
Entropy contributes to stabilization of multimetallic phases in high-temperature HEA nanoparticle synthesis.
The mechanism may not apply to low-temperature routes because equilibrium thermodynamics dominates there.
The mechanism may not apply when the constituent metal precursors have substantially dissimilar chemistries.
The cooling-rate threshold required to avoid phase separation varies with metal identity and precursor/support chemistry.
Equipment limitations and thermal gradients during quenching can impair reproducibility.

contradictions.description: The intervention places quenching after a high-temperature exposure that has already induced precursor decomposition, and the mechanism also states that all precursors decompose at high temperature. It then attributes the quench effect to preventing each precursor from reducing at its own rate. If reduction/decomposition has already occurred before quenching, the proposed quench cannot suppress those precursor-reduction rates without an additional explanation that reduction continues during cooling.
